Let’s dive into Chapter 7: the pitfalls of price controls and wage laws.
You know, governments often step in with things like minimum wage rules or rent ceilings, hoping to help folks who might be struggling—like low-income workers or renters.
But what if those good intentions actually lead to bigger problems?
Here’s something to pay attention to: when the government sets a maximum price—say, for rent—it can actually cause shortages. Why? Well, if landlords can’t charge enough, some might just stop renting out apartments, or they might let the quality slide.
On the flip side, if there’s a minimum price, like with a minimum wage, you often end up with a surplus. In other words, there are more people looking for jobs than there are jobs available, because employers either hire fewer people or start turning to automation instead.
And let’s not forget about black markets. When official channels aren’t working, people find ways around the rules. That means the original goal of the policy—helping those in need—can get completely undermined.
Think about rent control in a big city. Sure, some tenants benefit at first. But over time, landlords have less reason to keep buildings in good shape or to build new apartments. The end result? Fewer places to live, worse conditions, and a lot of people left out in the cold—literally.
The same logic applies to minimum wage laws. If the wage is set too high, the folks who need jobs the most—like young people just starting out, or those without much experience—might not even get a chance.
Sure, some workers see bigger paychecks. But the unseen victims? They’re the ones who never get hired at all.
So, what’s the big takeaway here? Well-intentioned rules can sometimes make things worse if we don’t look past the obvious and consider all the ripple effects.
When prices and wages can move freely, resources usually end up where they’re needed most—and that’s what helps everyone in the long run.
